drills.q: What single fact in a VPC determines whether a subnet is public or private?
drills.a: The subnet's route table -- specifically whether its default route (0.0.0.0/0) points at an Internet Gateway (public) or a NAT Gateway / nothing (private). The subnet itself has no inherent public/private property.

drills.q: A private subnet's app reads heavily from S3 and the NAT gateway bill has tripled. What's the fix and why is it free?
drills.a: Add a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3, associated with the private subnet's route table. It's implemented as a route-table entry (no ENI, no hourly or per-GB charge), and it keeps the traffic on the AWS backbone instead of through the NAT gateway at $0.045/GB.

drills.q: Explain, mechanically, why a NACL that only allows inbound port 443 breaks a working connection even though the security group is correctly configured.
drills.a: NACLs are stateless -- allowing inbound 443 says nothing about the response. The response leaves the server on an ephemeral source port; unless the NACL has a matching outbound allow rule for the ephemeral port range (roughly 1024-65535), that outbound packet is dropped. The SG is irrelevant here because SGs are stateful and would have allowed the return traffic automatically -- the NACL is evaluated independently and blocks it anyway.

drills.q: A partner requires a static IP allowlist entry for your HTTP API, which currently runs behind an ALB with path-based routing to three microservices. Design the fix.
drills.a: Put an NLB in front of the ALB using the 'ALB' target type, and allocate Elastic IPs to the NLB (one per AZ). The static IP satisfies the partner's allowlist requirement while the ALB behind it continues doing the path-based routing across the three services. A plain NLB alone can't do path routing; a plain ALB alone can't guarantee a static IP.

drills.q: You have 12 VPCs across 4 teams, all needing transitive connectivity to each other plus hybrid VPN access to on-prem. Peering or Transit Gateway, and why?
drills.a: Transit Gateway. Peering is non-transitive and would require up to 66 pairwise connections (12*11/2) with independently maintained route tables. Transit Gateway gives every VPC one attachment to a hub with transitive routing to all others, centralized per-attachment route control (so prod/staging can still be segmented), and a single place to fan out the VPN/Direct Connect hybrid connection to all 12 VPCs.

drills.q: Why does PrivateLink support overlapping CIDR ranges between provider and consumer VPCs when Peering and Transit Gateway do not?
drills.a: PrivateLink is a proxy, not a routing merge -- the consumer's interface endpoint is just an ENI in the consumer's own VPC that forwards to the provider's service over AWS's internal PrivateLink infrastructure. Neither side ever needs to route packets directly into the other's CIDR space, so there's no CIDR conflict possible. Peering and Transit Gateway both work by merging route tables across VPCs, which fails immediately if the CIDRs overlap.

drills.q: Diagnose: an ALB's health checks are passing, but 30% of requests to one target return connection refused, and it correlates with a recent NACL change locking down the private subnet.
drills.a: Check whether the NACL's outbound rules still allow the ephemeral port range back to the ALB subnet -- a partial/asymmetric NACL lockdown can drop return traffic for some but not all connections depending on load balancer node placement across AZs. Also verify the NACL wasn't accidentally scoped to block traffic between AZs within the same VPC if the ALB nodes and targets aren't co-located.

drills.q: Why is 'anycast beats DNS for fast failover' true even when your Route53 TTL is set to 5 seconds?
drills.a: TTL is a request to caching resolvers and clients, not an enforced contract. OS-level resolvers, corporate/ISP resolvers, and some client stacks cache longer than instructed or apply their own minimums, so a 5s TTL doesn't guarantee 5s propagation across your actual client population. Anycast (e.g. Global Accelerator) sidesteps this because failover happens by withdrawing/rerouting at the network layer, which every client observes without any cache to expire.

drills.q: Design network isolation for a shared internal recommendation API consumed by 20 independent product teams' VPCs, some of which use the same CIDR range (10.0.0.0/16) by historical accident.
drills.a: PrivateLink. Put the API behind an NLB, create a VPC endpoint service, and have each of the 20 consumer VPCs create an interface endpoint into it. Since PrivateLink doesn't merge routing tables, the overlapping 10.0.0.0/16 CIDRs across consumer VPCs are a non-issue -- Peering or Transit Gateway would both fail outright or require re-IP'ing several teams' VPCs first.

drills.q: A gRPC service behind an ALB shows p99 8ms higher than an identical NLB-fronted deployment. Should you switch, and what's the actual decision criterion?
drills.a: Not automatically -- the criterion is whether you're using ALB's L7 features (host/path routing across services, ACM-managed TLS termination, WAF). If yes, an 8ms overhead against inference calls that take hundreds of milliseconds is very unlikely to be the real bottleneck, and the operational simplicity of ALB usually wins. If the service is genuinely latency-critical (sub-millisecond budget matters, e.g. a bidding system) and doesn't need L7 routing, switch to NLB.

drills.q: Given a route table with 0.0.0.0/0 -> NAT Gateway in AZ-a, and a private subnet in AZ-b routing through that same NAT gateway, what two costs does this incur beyond normal NAT charges, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: Cross-AZ data transfer charges (roughly $0.01/GB each direction) on top of the NAT's own per-GB processing charge, plus a single point of failure -- if the AZ-a NAT gateway or its AZ has an outage, AZ-b's private subnet loses outbound connectivity too. Fix: deploy one NAT gateway per AZ and route each private subnet to its own-AZ NAT gateway.
